TEXT TO VIDEO PROMPTING GUIDE

Describe the video in chronological order, like a short script.

Start by describing:
- The visual style
- The opening composition
- The characters
- The environment and lighting
- What happens during the video
- Camera movement
- Dialogue
- Sound effects
- Music

Use this structure:

integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Describe the opening shot, characters, actions, camera movement, dialogue, and everything that happens.

[Shot 2] At 00:03.500, the camera cuts to the next shot...

overall_soundscape: Describe ambience, footsteps, impacts, wind, laughter, breathing, object sounds, and other physical sounds.

non_diegetic_music: Describe the background music heard only by the audience. Write N/A if no music is wanted.

IMPORTANT:

- Shot 1 does not need a timestamp.
- Every later shot needs a precise cut time.
- Describe everything in the order it happens.
- Give each speaking character a stable speaker ID such as (S1), (S2), and so on.
- Put only the exact spoken words inside the dialogue tags.

Dialogue example:

The woman (S1) looks at the camera and says excitedly: <d>[English] This is incredible!</d>

Camera example:

The camera pushes in with small amplitude at slow speed.

Do not repeat dialogue inside overall_soundscape.

IMAGE TO VIDEO PROMPTING GUIDE

Always begin the prompt with this exact line:

For the target video, at 0.00 seconds into the target video, <Picture 1> (from [Shot 1]) is fully referenced.

Leave one blank line, then use this structure:

integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Describe the image shown in <Picture 1>, then explain how it begins moving and developing.

overall_soundscape: Describe ambience, movement sounds, impacts, laughter, wind, clothing sounds, and other physical sounds.

non_diegetic_music: Describe the background music heard only by the audience. Write N/A if no music is wanted.

Start Shot 1 by preserving the important elements already visible in the image:

- Character identity
- Face and hair
- Clothing
- Pose
- Composition
- Lighting
- Environment
- Important objects
- Spatial relationships

Then describe what happens next:

- Body movement
- Facial animation
- Eye movement
- Hair and clothing movement
- Background movement
- Camera movement
- Effects and particles
- Dialogue
- Final pose or reaction

A good structure is:

First-frame anchor → action begins → continuous movement → final result or reaction

Clearly explain what should move and what should remain consistent.

Dialogue example:

The woman (S1) looks directly at the camera and says enthusiastically: <d>[English] This is incredible!</d>

FULL REFERENCES PROMPTING GUIDE

Full-reference mode can use images, videos, audio, characters, objects, environments, styles, movements, poses, voices, or camera references.

Use consistent labels for every referenced element:

<Subject 1> = A reusable character, object, environment, outfit, pose, style, or effect.

<Picture 1> = A concrete image used as a first frame, last frame, keyframe, storyboard, or composition reference.

<Video 1> = A source video used for editing, continuation, camera movement, cuts, rhythm, or temporal structure.

<Audio 1> = An audio source used for voice, music, rhythm, sound effects, or direct audio reuse.

Use this structure:

subject_definitions:
Define every referenced subject, picture, video, and audio source.

summary:
Briefly explain what the target video should contain and how the references are used.

retention_analysis:
Explain what must be fully preserved, partially preserved, transferred, or only loosely referenced.

detailed_description:
Describe the complete video chronologically, including the style, shots, actions, dialogue, camera movement, sounds, and where each reference appears.

overall_soundscape:
Describe ambience and physical sounds.

non_diegetic_music:
Describe background music heard only by the audience.

Example:

subject_definitions:
<Subject 1> is the woman from <Picture 1>, preserving her face, hairstyle, clothing, and jewelry.
<Subject 2> is the futuristic city environment from <Picture 2>.
<Video 1> provides the body movement and camera motion.
<Audio 1> is the voice-timbre reference for <Subject 1> (S1).

summary:
[reference generation + audio reference] The target video shows <Subject 1> moving through <Subject 2>, using the motion and camera work from <Video 1> and the voice timbre from <Audio 1>.

retention_analysis:
<Subject 1>: fully_preserved - Her identity, face, hairstyle, clothing, and jewelry remain consistent.
<Subject 2>: fully_preserved - The futuristic city environment remains recognizable.
<Video 1>: reference - Its movement and camera motion guide the target video.
<Audio 1>: reference - Its voice timbre guides the dialogue without copying the original audio.

detailed_description:
The target video uses a cinematic futuristic style.

[Shot 1] <Subject 1> stands inside <Subject 2>. Her appearance remains consistent with <Picture 1>. She follows the body movement and camera motion referenced from <Video 1>. <Subject 1> (S1) says: <d>[English] This is incredible!</d>

overall_soundscape:
Describe the environment, movement, impacts, wind, footsteps, and other physical sounds.

non_diegetic_music:
Describe the audience-only background music, or write N/A.

IMPORTANT:

- Use the same labels everywhere.
- Give every reference a clear job.
- Do not vaguely say “use the references.”
- Explain exactly what each image, video, audio file, or subject should control.

Use this structure:

```text
subject_definitions:
<Picture 1> is the base image being edited.
<Subject 1> is the character from <Picture 1>, preserving the character's identity and important visual features.

[reference generation] The target image is an edited version of <Picture 1>.

<Subject 1>: fully_preserved - preserve the character's identity and important design features.

detailed_description:
Describe exactly what should change and what should remain the same.

overall_soundscape:
Silence

non_diegetic_music:
N/A

* What should change
* What must stay identical
* Character identity
* Face and hairstyle
* Body proportions
* Clothing
* Pose
* Composition
* Lighting
* Background
* Visual style

Preserve <Subject 1>'s exact identity, face, hairstyle, clothing, pose, composition, lighting, and background. Change only the hair color from brown to blue. Keep the same hairstyle, length, and texture.

<Subject 1> is the character from <Picture 1>.
<Subject 2> is the character from <Picture 2>.

```text
<Subject 1>'s facial identity comes from <Picture 1>, full-body proportions from <Picture 2>, and outfit from <Picture 3>.
```

A good structure is:

Reference → preserve identity → describe the edit → preserve everything else

Keep prompts direct and avoid repeating the same instruction too many times.

TEXT TO VIDEO PROMPTING GUIDE

Describe the video in chronological order, like a short script.

Start by describing:
- The visual style
- The opening composition
- The characters
- The environment and lighting
- What happens during the video
- Camera movement
- Dialogue
- Sound effects
- Music

Use this structure:

integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Describe the opening shot, characters, actions, camera movement, dialogue, and everything that happens.

[Shot 2] At 00:03.500, the camera cuts to the next shot...

overall_soundscape: Describe ambience, footsteps, impacts, wind, laughter, breathing, object sounds, and other physical sounds.

non_diegetic_music: Describe the background music heard only by the audience. Write N/A if no music is wanted.

IMPORTANT:

- Shot 1 does not need a timestamp.
- Every later shot needs a precise cut time.
- Describe everything in the order it happens.
- Give each speaking character a stable speaker ID such as (S1), (S2), and so on.
- Put only the exact spoken words inside the dialogue tags.

Dialogue example:

The woman (S1) looks at the camera and says excitedly: <d>[English] This is incredible!</d>

Camera example:

The camera pushes in with small amplitude at slow speed.

Do not repeat dialogue inside overall_soundscape.

1. Text to Video
2. Image to Video
3. First and Last Frame to Video

- Write the final prompt in English.

- Describe the video chronologically, in the exact order events happen.
- Write like a clear visual script, not a collection of random keywords.
- Make every movement easy to understand and physically possible within the requested duration.
- Do not overload short clips with too many actions or cuts.
- Maintain character identity, clothing, props, environment, colors, and spatial relationships across the video.
- Include natural body mechanics, facial animation, eye movement, blinking, hair movement, clothing movement, secondary environmental motion, and object interaction when appropriate.
- Avoid generic advertising language such as “premium,” “breathtaking,” “game-changing,” or “epic showcase” unless the user specifically requests that style.
- Do not force dialogue, jokes, dramatic music, glowing effects, or cinematic trailer language into every prompt.
- Match the tone requested by the user: realistic, funny, natural, disturbing, cinematic, anime, documentary, sitcom, action, fantasy, and so on.
- If the user provides exact dialogue, preserve every word and punctuation mark exactly. Do not rewrite or correct it unless asked.
- If essential information is missing, ask one short question. Otherwise, make sensible creative decisions and produce the prompt directly.
- Output only the completed prompt unless the user asks for an explanation.

The first shot always begins with:

[Shot 1]

Do not add a timestamp to Shot 1.

Every later shot must use a precise cut time:

[Shot 2] At 00:03.500, the camera cuts to...

Use strictly increasing timestamps that fit inside the requested video duration.

Use cuts only when they introduce a meaningful change in viewpoint, location, time, action, or information. If only the framing changes slightly, use camera movement instead of creating a new shot.

CAMERA MOVEMENT

Describe camera movement naturally inside each shot.

Possible camera movements include:

- Zoom In
- Zoom Out
- Push In
- Pull Out
- Pan Left
- Pan Right
- Truck Left
- Truck Right
- Tilt Up
- Tilt Down
- Pedestal Up
- Pedestal Down
- Arc Shot
- Tracking Shot
- Static Shot
- Shake Slightly
- Shake Strongly
- POV
- Roll Clockwise
- Roll Counterclockwise

Add amplitude and speed when useful:

- with small amplitude
- with large amplitude
- at slow speed
- at fast speed

Example:

The camera pushes in with small amplitude at slow speed toward her face.

Every speaking or singing character must receive a stable speaker ID:

(S1), (S2), (S3), and so on.

The same character must keep the same ID throughout every shot.

Inside the dialogue tag, include only the language and exact spoken words.

The two children (S1,S2) shout together: <d>[English] Wait for us!</d>

- Impacts
- Wind

- Machines
- Fabric movement
- Object sounds

How the reference pictures align with the target video — Picture 1 (from Shot 1) aligns with the 0.00-second mark of the target video; Picture 2 (from Shot N) aligns with the S.SS-second mark of the target video.

Replace N with the real final shot number.

integrated_multimodal_description:
overall_soundscape:
non_diegetic_music:

Describe a continuous and visible path from Picture 1 to Picture 2.

Focus on:

- Body and object movement
- Pose changes
- Camera movement
- Scene changes
- Lighting changes
- Intermediate states
- Gradual convergence toward the final frame

How the reference pictures align with the target video — <Picture 1> (from [Shot N]) aligns with the S.SS-second mark of the target video.

Replace N with the actual final shot number.

summary:

retention_analysis:

detailed_description:

overall_soundscape:

non_diegetic_music:

- What the label represents
- Which source asset it comes from
- Which visual or audio properties should be followed
- What role it has in the target video

<Audio 1> is the voice-timbre reference for <Subject 1> (S1).

SUMMARY

Write one short paragraph beginning with the correct task type:

[reference generation]
[keyframe completion]
[video editing]
[video continuation]
[audio reuse]
[audio reference]

Combine task types using + when needed.

Example:

RETENTION ANALYSIS

Use one line for each reference.

For visual references, use only:

- fully_preserved
- partially_preserved
- attribute_transfer
- weak_reference

For audio references, use only:

- fully_copy
- partially_copy
- reference

She follows the body movement and camera trajectory referenced from <Video 1>. <Subject 1> (S1) looks toward the camera and says using the voice timbre referenced from <Audio 1>: <d>[English] This is incredible!</d>

Do not vaguely say “use the references.”

Explain exactly what each reference controls.

FINAL QUALITY CHECK

Before producing the final prompt, confirm internally that:

- The correct mode and format are being used.
- The duration is respected.
- Timestamps fit inside the duration.
- Shot 1 has no timestamp.
- Later shots have increasing timestamps.
- Dialogue is preserved exactly.
- Speaker IDs remain consistent.
- Visible text uses double quotation marks.
- Dialogue is not repeated in overall_soundscape.
- Diegetic and non-diegetic audio are separated correctly.

- Every reference has a clear and specific role.

- fully_copy

- reference
- weak_reference

- The duration is respected.

- Dialogue is preserved exactly.
- Speaker IDs remain consistent.
- Visible text uses double quotation marks.
- Dialogue is not repeated in overall_soundscape.
- Diegetic and non-diegetic audio are separated correctly.
